tn.quote: This is the most commonly heard pattern. Each word in the utterance, including nonsyllabic words, takes a primary stress. (Stress is nonphonemic and occurs on the penultimate syllable of all words of more than one syllable.) The intonation contour remains level until the penultimate syllable of the final word. Pitch rises on the penultimate syllable, then falls again on the next syllable to the original level unless it is utterance final, in which case it drops yet another level.

3596.prule: Each lexical word (noun, verb, adjective, adverb) carries exactly one primary prominence, analysed by Carter as one underlying high tone H realised as high pitch on the primary-stressed syllable. Its position in the word is lexically fixed and distinctive (turkéy 'bird' vs Túrkey 'country'; Holder: practice vs practice, baker vs Bàkèr), with 'no preference for certain patterns over others'; many words keep the English position, many others place H one or two syllables further right (storý, jackét, watér, hospítal, coconút, organíze). No positional or weight rule is stated.
3596.srule: Holder 1999 (sect. 3.1-3.4 pp. 61-64): a word may carry two or more accents; the rightmost is the main accent (H*), the others are toneless foot-level secondary accents on the heads of the preceding trochaic or unary feet (ònomàtopéia every second syllable; Dèmerára, kìndergárten, àlligátor, hùrricáne; adjacent to the main accent with a unary foot: bàmbóo, bàndána, òrchéstra); unfooted syllables carry none (Ja(pán), ba(nána), A(méri)ca) and footing is word-specific; in the learned class with penultimate-foot main accent the final foot head stays secondary (ozone, anecdote). Carter 1987 (sect. 2.2 p. 258) only notes that Holder showed 'more than one degree' of stress and gives no placement.
3596.quote: Holder’s work has demonstrated the importance of stress, and the existence of more than one degree of this feature; nevertheless, I propose here to describe Guyanese in terms of a tonal system. The association of stress and pitch is such that any syllable with primary stress has surface high pitch, though not all surface high pitches are analyzed as having underlying H.[8] [...] As noted under 2.1, tone has lexically distinctive function in Guyanese. The minimal pair recorded by Allsopp (1972) is supported by Holder (in press): turkéy (bird) and Túrkey (country). [...] 2.6.1 Uncompounded item…
3596.idn: Guyanese “English-based” Creole, or “Creolese” (Carter); 'anglais est-caribéen... parler... de la Guyana' / 'anglo-guyanais' (Holder 1999); data: No fieldwork locality or dates stated: Carter's material is a recording of Dennis Craig's 1982 conference paper plus word material and recordings supplied by Maurice Holder…
3596.exq_: Carter states no positional rule (‘no preference for certain patterns over others’), so exceptions do not arise. For Holder's metrical generalisation (1999: 63-64): ‘Cependant, il y a un certain nombre de vocables qui ne se conforment pas entièrement à ce patron: en N2 c’est l’accent pénultième qui…
3596.tone: Carter analyses Guyanese as a ditonemic (H/L) tonal system built on stress: primary stress = underlying H, one H per word/tone-group, other syllables L (surface h by progressive assimilation), downstep/downdrift at group junctures; note 8 records Holder's observation that this makes Guyanese a pitch-accent language. Holder 1999 treats tone as predictable from accent ('la previsibilite du ton a partir de l'accent'): accent 1 = H* on the strong syllable, accent 2 = B*H (lexically marked, mostly disyllables, list in appendix); one tonal accent per 'groupe accentuel'; contrasts this eastern-Caribbean accentual system with Jamaican's fixed/variable tone words. APiCS (Devonish & Thompson) codes Creolese feature 120 as 'reduced tone system' with minimal pairs from Devonish 1989: 94 (pákìit 'packet' vs pàkít 'pocket'). The system type is a stress-anchored pitch accent; the placement question the catalog asks is lexical.

Stated as a tendency, not a rule; the same page's example neyabarakueikueijei has the accent on the penult (itself a triphthong syllable) although the final syllable is also a diphthong. Coda consonants and plain vowel length are not mentioned as weight. Kerr 1995 states no weight condition at all.
3600.prule: Primary word accent falls by default on the penultimate syllable of the word (Kerr 1995 p. 22 'generalmente cae en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra'; Kerr & Berg 2018 p. 12 'Generalmente el acento primario cae en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra, si no, está marcado'); syllables whose nucleus is a diphthong or triphthong tend to attract the accent, most often the one nearest the end of the word (Kerr & Berg 2018 p. 13, stated as a tendency: 'se inclina', 'frecuentemente'). Kerr 1995 adds that the position of the main accent varies and 'las reglas no son tan sencillas'. A few minimal pairs are distinguished by accent alone (narúntaba/naruntaba, taxotsi/táxotsi, kekoba/kékoba) and some words vary (wámonae/wamonae). Merchán 2000 (Maibén variant) independently: accent preferentially penultimate, predictable, with a few final and antepenultimate words.
3600.srule: Long polymorphemic words have one primary accent (generally penultimate) and may have several secondary accents; the dictionary places these on the component roots and affixes, whose own accents are shown in each entry's V. cross-references (naitabara-ikika < na-, -ítabara, ikika). No positional or rhythmic rule is given. (Kerr 1995 sec. 0-6 p. 22 and Merchán 2000 p. 587 do not mention secondary accent.)

3601.prule: Stress is a contrastive suprasegmental phoneme that falls only on the final or the penultimate syllable of the word; within that two-syllable right-edge window its position is lexically fixed and not otherwise predictable (minimal pair dúhci 'maize' vs duhcí 'to see'; iwililúmɨ 'river' penultimate). Every word, including compounds, carries exactly one stress.

3603.prule: Root-penultimate pitch accent with morphological conditioning: a right-to-left metrical grid is built over the morphological root (domain = 'a raiz morfológica') and the accent is lexically assigned to the penultimate syllable of the root; suffixes lexically marked < > are extrametrical, and that extrametricality is cancelled when a further suffix follows (non-exhaustivity), so the surface position ranges over the last four syllables of the phonological word (final [ku.ɻĩ́m] 'não' to pre-antepenultimate [ma.tʃi.já.pa.ɻu.pe] 'boas, bonitas', p. 53-54). 3605.dq: Word stress in CMA occurs wherever Old Arabic displayed long syllables. In CMA stress falls most often on penultimate syllables and thus need not need be indicated in this position.
3605.dloc: Borg 2008, pp. 1-2: the stress paragraph closes p. 1 ('Word stress in CMA occurs... where it falls') and its example line ('on initial or final syllables pkyínixtep... maxtúp') opens p. 2.
3605.heavy: Diachronic only: 'Word stress in CMA occurs wherever Old Arabic displayed long syllables' (Borg 2008), while synchronically 'CMA has no long vowels' (Borg 2008; Walter 2020: 165 'the Arabic vowel length contrast has also been lost'); consonant length survives as gemination. Tsiapera 1969: 16 (carried via Shormani 2023) had stated that long vowels and word-final VCC syllables attract stress; the long-vowel clause is vacuous or circular in the modern language and the final-VCC clause is carried only.
3605.dflt: penult ('In CMA stress falls most often on penultimate syllables'); marked positions are initial (pkyínixtep; the verb-nucleus words of Borg 2006 via Shormani, e.g. tàxakilla, initial in a four-syllable word) or final (maxtúp; Tsiapera's final-VCC words raxímt, mindàxt via Shormani).
3605.prule: Lexically fixed stress with a penult default (Borg 2008, first-hand): 'Word stress in CMA occurs wherever Old Arabic displayed long syllables', but 'CMA has no long vowels', so the conditioning is etymological, not synchronic surface weight; stress 'falls most often on penultimate syllables' and otherwise on the initial or final syllable of particular words (pkyínixtep 'he is being inscribed', maxtúp 'written'). Under the paper's own convention (penult stress left unmarked) kadder 'he measured' is penult-stressed while maxtúp 'written' is final-stressed, both CVC.CVC on the surface, so placement is not computable from synchronic syllable weight.

Word stress, accent or prominence is never mentioned, located or denied.
